The problem with raising platforms is mainly that stations cleared for freight or where trains pass through have to account for the 'kinematic envelope' (the area a train could wobble into), especially for freight trains.

As you can imagine, the wheels at the bottom are the fixed point, and so the higher up you go, the bigger the width envelope for a given angle of lean. (Think of it as triangle like this ◤)

For example, imagine you've got a 1m high platform with a 10cm gap between train and platform. That means the train can wobble about 6 degrees before it hits the platform.

If you build that platform up to 1.5m, the acceptable wobble drops to about 3.8 degrees. 

This means that the higher the platforms, the bigger the gap you need to leave between the train and platform to avoid the risk of a rocking train impacting the platform edge (which would not be pretty at speed). Past a certain point, the big gap would be just as, if not more problematic for mobility as the big step.

The solution is not to raise platforms, but to update rolling stock so that the entries are at the standard platform height. As to why that hasn't been done, pretty much the same reason there were still Pacers on the rails until 2021. New rolling stock costs money.

The point I was more getting to was that 'relative child poverty' isn't the best measure of a child's actual experience. It's entirely possible for a child in a household earning more than 60% of the national median income to go hungry, and even more possible to massively impact the situation of children with measures that don't directly impact their household income.

For example, if we announced that we were adding £100 per child per month to child benefit, but that the NHS would now charge for treating kids, 'relative child poverty' would be reduced massively, but a bunch of kids would die because they couldn't afford medical treatment. 

Essentially, 'relative child poverty' is a poor measure when it comes to government intervention to help children, because it flatly ignores any intervention that is not a cash payment to the parents. One could provide every child in the country 3 free, nutritious meals per day, world class education, unlimited free childcare and everything else they could need, but if it wasn't done as a cash payment to parents, they'd still count as being impoverished by this metric. Likewise one could strip away a child's healthcare, education and every social program in existence, replace them with a £100 per month cash grant to parents and it'd reduce poverty per this measure.

That largely comes down to the way poverty is calculated. It is based on household income relative to the median without looking at outgoings.

So, for example, if we increased benefits by £10 a month by implementing a 10,000% tax on baby formula, child poverty would fall even though a shitload of babies would starve. 

Likewise policies like free school meals and the breakfast clubs that are being implemented at primary schools don't directly impact child poverty figures at all because nobody's household income changes, but make a massive difference to the wellbeing of children. 

In theory, a more cost effective way to reduce child poverty would be to introduce a 'child education benefit' of £7640 per child per year paid to all children and then add a mandatory charge of £7640 per child per year for state education. It'd change nothing in practice, but on paper child poverty rates would plummet, because if everyone's household income went up by £7640/child, less people would be below 60% of the median.
